questions.problem:
Which of the following ordered pairs is a solution to $y=-\frac{x}{6}?$

I. $(-18,-3)$

II. $(6,1)$

III. $(12,-2)$
questions.worked_solution:
To check whether each point is a solution to the equation, we substitute it into the equation and see if it results in a true statement.

First, we substitute $(-18,-3)$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{x}{6} \\ (-3) & =-\frac{(-18)}{6} \\ -3 & =3\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

The result is a false statement, so $(-18,-3)$ is *not* a solution to the equation.

Next, we substitute $(6,1)$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{x}{6} \\ (1) & =-\frac{6}{6} \\ 1 & =-1\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

The result is again a false statement, so $(6,1)$ is also *not* a solution to the equation.

Finally, we substitute $(12,-2)$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{x}{6} \\ (-2) & =-\frac{12}{6} \\ -2 & =-2\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

The result is a true statement, so $(12,-2)$ is a solution to the equation.

So, out of the three ordered pairs given, the only pair that is a solution to the equation is III $(12,-2).$

questions.problem:
Which of the following ordered pairs is a solution to $y=2x-3?$

I. $(-2,-7)$

II. $(0,3)$

III. $(2,4)$
questions.worked_solution:
To check whether each point is a solution to the equation, we substitute it into the equation and see if it results in a true statement.

First, we substitute $(-2,-7)$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2x-3 \\ (-7) & =2(-2)-3 \\ -7 & =-4-3 \\ -7 & =-7\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

The result is a true statement, so $(-2,-7)$ is a solution to the equation.

Next, we substitute $(0,3)$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2x-3 \\ (3) & =2(0)-3 \\ 3 & =-3\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

The result is a false statement, so $(0,3)$ is *not* a solution to the equation.

Finally, we substitute $(2,4)$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2x-3 \\ (4) & =2(2)-3 \\ 4 & =4-3 \\ 4 & =1\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

The result is again a false statement, so $(2,4)$ is also *not* a solution to the equation.

So, out of the three ordered pairs given, the only pair that is a solution to the equation is I $(-2,-7).$

questions.problem: A solution to the linear equation $3x-4y=2$ is the ordered pair $(-2,k).$ What is the value of $k?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $(-2,k)$ is a solution to the linear equation $3x-4y=2,$ the equation must turn into a true statement if we substitute $-2$ and $k$ for $x$ and $y.$ So, we replace $x$ with $-2$ and $y$ with $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-4y & =2 \\ 3(-2)-4(k) & =2 \\ -6-4k & =2 \\ -4k & =8 \\ k & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A solution to the linear equation $y=4x-11$ is the ordered pair $(2,h).$ What is the value of $h?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $(2,h)$ is a solution to the linear equation $y=4x-11,$ the equation must turn into a true statement if we substitute $2$ and $h$ for $x$ and $y.$ So, we replace $x$ with $2$ and $y$ with $h,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =4x-11 \\ (h) & =4(2)-11 \\ h & =8-11 \\ h & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Example: 
                    Identifying a Solution to a Given Equation
canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the given points is a solution to $y=-2x+1?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14165646/assets/b921dae09304534b2176dbc7a74c75c4ab36c76c67edb6b97cbe358bc703c6b5.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The plotted points correspond to the $xy$-pairs $A(-1, 3)$ and $B(2,-4).$ To check whether each point is a solution to the equation, we substitute it into the equation and see if it results in a true statement.

First, we substitute $A(-1,3)$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-2x+1 \\ (3) & =-2(-1)+1 \\ 3 & =3\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

The result is a true statement, so $A(-1,3)$ is a solution to the equation.

Next, we substitute $B(2,-4)$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-2x+1 \\ (-4) & =-2(2)+1 \\ -4 & =-4+1 \\ -4 & =-3\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

The result is a false statement, so $B(2,-4)$ is *not* solution to the equation.

Therefore, only $A(-1,3)$ is a solution to the equation.

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding a Missing Coordinate in a Solution
canonical_examples.problem: A solution to the linear equation $y-5x=2$ is the ordered pair $(2,k).$ What is the value of $k?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since $(2,k)$ is a solution to the linear equation $y-5x=2,$ the equation must turn into a true statement if we substitute $2$ and $k$ for $x$ and $y.$ So, we replace $x$ with $2$ and $y$ with $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-5x & =2 \\ (k)-5(2) & =2 \\ k-10 & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we solve for $k\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}k-10 & =2 \\ k & =12\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
A **linear equation** in the variables $x$ and $y$ is an equation that involves just these two variables, possibly with some constants. There should be no powers on any of the variables and the variables can't be multiplied together.

For example, the following are linear equations:

$$
y = x + 4, \qquad
	y = -3x, \qquad
	5y = 6x,\qquad
	2x + 3y = 9
$$

On the other hand, the following are *not* linear equations:

$$
y = x^2 - 2x, \qquad
	y^2 = - 4x + 2, \qquad
	y = 2xy
$$

A **solution** of a linear equation is an **ordered pair** $(x,y)$ that makes the equation true. 

For instance, the ordered pair $(3, 7)$ is a solution to the equation $y = 3x - 2$ because if we replace $x$ with $3$ and $y$ with $7,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3x-2 \\ (7) & =3(3)-2 \\ 7 & =9-2 \\ 7 & =7\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

The above is a true statement, so $(3, 7)$ is a solution to the equation $y = 3x - 2.$

**Important**: A linear equation in two variables has an infinite number of solutions, not just one!
